vignette:
She is 66, a South Asian woman who has spent most of her adult life being the person others lean on. For years she has worked as a security guard in a large office complex, taking the early shift whenever she can. She likes the structure of the job—the routine of checking doors, watching the monitors, logging visitors in a careful hand. She says that before everything happened, she was known for being steady. “Nothing shakes me,” she used to tell her husband.

What changes her is not something that happens to her directly, but to her younger son.

Two years ago, on a humid evening, she is at home preparing dinner when the phone rings. At first she almost ignores it, thinking he will call back. Instead she answers and hears a stranger’s voice telling her there has been an accident. Her son has been badly injured after a violent assault outside the shop where he works. She remembers dropping the spoon, remembers not understanding the words the first time they are said, then suddenly hearing everything too clearly—the hospital name, the urgency, the instruction to come quickly.

She still talks about that drive as if it is happening now. Her husband is beside her, but she barely registers him. The streetlights smear in her vision. In the emergency department she sees blood on her son’s shirt, his face swollen in a way that makes him look both familiar and unrecognizable. She cannot stop staring at his chest to make sure it rises. Even now, when she tells the story, this is the point where she presses a hand to her own sternum, as if trying to force air into herself.

Her son survives, but the weeks that follow are full of operations, uncertainty, and long hours by his bedside. She sleeps upright in a plastic chair, waking at every machine sound. She begins to expect bad news at any moment. Whenever a doctor approaches, her stomach drops. Family members praise her strength because she manages phone calls, meals, prayer arrangements, and updates to relatives overseas. Inside, she feels as if she is standing on broken glass.

After her son comes home, everyone expects life to settle. Instead, she finds that the hospital has followed her. At work, the surveillance monitors pull her back to that first terrible phone call. A man running through the lobby, two people arguing in the parking lot, an ambulance passing the building—each one sends a bolt through her body. She becomes more watchful than the job requires. She checks exits repeatedly, startles when someone comes up behind her, and scans faces for danger. Her coworkers joke that she sees trouble before it starts. She laughs with them, but her shoulders remain tight for hours.

Sleep becomes thin and unreliable. She lies down exhausted, then sees her son as he was that night, blood at his collar, eyes half open. Sometimes she dreams that the phone is ringing and ringing, and when she answers no one speaks. On those nights she gets up before dawn and irons her uniform or wipes down the kitchen counters because being still feels unbearable. Her husband tells her she is wearing herself out. She snaps at him for small things, then feels ashamed and goes quiet.

She avoids the neighborhood where the assault happened, even if it means taking a longer route to work. If her son is late answering a message, her mind jumps instantly to catastrophe. She calls again, then again. She knows he is an adult; she knows she sounds overbearing. Still, when she finally hears his voice, her knees weaken with relief. She watches him closely at family gatherings, noticing every wince, every tired expression, as if his body might reveal some hidden damage that everyone else has missed.

What troubles her most is how much her world has narrowed. She used to enjoy temple visits, crowded weddings, noisy family dinners. Now crowded places make her uneasy. She sits near exits, tracks unfamiliar men with her eyes, and urges everyone to leave early. She feels guilty because she is grateful her son is alive, yet she cannot reclaim the sense of safety she once carried so naturally. She tells herself she should be over it by now. Instead she feels trapped between the past and the present—her son sitting in front of her, healed in many ways, and at the same time the image of him on that hospital bed remaining as vivid as if she has just walked into the room.
